analysis.one_liner: Let people see, correct, and control who sees genetic records held by federal agencies.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors, never left House committee, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given people rights over genetic information held by federal agencies and their contractors: the right to see their own genetic records, get copies for free, correct errors, and require written authorization before any disclosure. Agencies could still share genetic information for treatment, emergencies, or court orders without permission. The bill never got a committee vote and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose genetic information ends up in a federal database — patients at government-run health facilities, participants in government-funded genetic research, and people identified through federal genetic testing. The bill's own findings warned that misuse of genetic records could cost people jobs, insurance, credit, and education [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with genetic records in federal databases

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals the right to inspect and copy any genetic information a government agency keeps about them, at no charge, with a response required within ten days [S3].
Lets people correct or supplement inaccurate genetic records, and requires agencies to attach the person's written disagreement to any later disclosure of disputed information [S3].
Bars agencies from disclosing genetic information to anyone without the individual's written, specific authorization, with civil suits and criminal penalties for violations [S3].
Extends the same protections to genetic information held by federal contractors and grantees, closing the loophole where private companies do the government's genetic work [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies and the contractors and grantees that maintain genetic data for them, who would face new compliance duties, notice requirements, and legal liability [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal agencies and genetics research contractors

drawbacks.text: The bill only covers government agencies and their contractors — it would do nothing about the biggest private-sector risks the findings themselves name: employers, insurers, and lenders misusing genetic information [S3].
Agencies could still share genetic information internally for official use, with treating medical professionals, in emergencies, and by court order without the individual's consent [S3].
Compliance costs, notice requirements, and liability exposure would fall on federal agencies and their research contractors, and the bill sets no funding for any of it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people whose genetic data sits in federal systems, the bill offered real, enforceable rights — access, correction, and consent — at a modest compliance cost to agencies. Its main weakness is scope: it left private employers and insurers, the users of genetic information most likely to affect someone's job or coverage, entirely unregulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Government Operations Committee and its subcommittees in April 1991, and nothing ever happened after that; it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. introduced the Human Genome Privacy Act on April 24, 1991, as concern grew over the federally funded Human Genome Project's ability to compile identifiable genetic data on individuals [S1][S3].
No representative signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Government Operations and then to two of its subcommittees on April 29, 1991, and no further action was ever taken [S1][S5].
The bill expired with the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993, without a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing on the record [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and their genetic-research contractors avoided new privacy obligations, record-access duties, and liability. Individuals whose genetic data flows through government systems gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies and their genetics contractors

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its genetic privacy framework; no other member joined him.

against.name: House Committee on Government Operations
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 24, 1991, referred it to subcommittees, and never brought it to a markup or vote.

against.name: Subcommittees on Government Information, Justice and Agriculture, and Legislation and National Security
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from April 29, 1991 onward and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no organized opposition or support from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have applied its access, correction, and consent rules to private companies doing genetic work under federal contract or grant, and made their employees liable like agency staff. Their interest in avoiding those obligations ran against individuals' control over their own genetic records.

Agencies would have faced new duties to give people access to their genetic records, publish notices of information practices, and answer for misuse in court. The bill also preserved agency flexibility to share genetic data internally, for treatment, and in emergencies without consent.
